Waiver moves, by title odds

Each pickup is priced in P(win the title) on the same simulated seasons: claiming now, against waiting and claiming only if he breaks out (you win that claim when your priority beats the other managers who also want him), less what your waiver priority is worth on future claims. Passing is not free: if he breaks out, a rival claims him, and what that does to your title odds is counted. Each move is priced on its own; make one, then refresh. Assumes about a third of active managers chase any one breakout. Injured free agents are priced as IR stashes: no roster spot until he is back, with the chance he never is.

Waiver plans: several moves together

Moves interact -- two backs chasing one lineup spot are worth less together, two dead roster spots turned into a starter and his handcuff can be worth more -- so every combination of two or three pickups and drops is screened, and the best priced in title odds against standing pat and against the best single move. Make the plan when it beats that single move by more than the simulation noise; a close call when by less.

No plan beats the best single move; make that one and refresh.

Pickups for this matchup

Every free agent who could start for you this week, added to your roster with your best lineup rebuilt around him and scored against your opponent on the same simulated games as your lineup as it stands -- the chance you win this week with him, against without. The title columns are the whole move in points of P(title), on the season simulation: Wk is this week's win -- the P(win) gain times what this game swings your title odds; Rest is every week after, his value less that of the player you drop; Net is the two together, less the waiver priority a claim spends. The verdict goes on Net: a pickup that wins this week can still cost more later than it gains now. If he is on waivers, the claim has to clear before his game.

Upside stashes

Could be worth is his ceiling a game in a month if things break his way (85th percentile of how projections move). Worth a bench spot you would otherwise waste.

Trades

Trades close in 8 days (Nov 11). After that only waiver moves can change your roster.

Every 1-for-1, 2-for-1 and 1-for-2 with every team, and 2-for-2 among each side's eight most valuable players; when a deal frees one of your roster spots, the free agent who adds most fills it and is priced in. For you: priced in title odds for both teams on the same simulated seasons as the waiver moves. For him: he cannot see this tool, so his side is judged the way the market values players -- the platform's projection, a player's name and last season, this season so far, injuries -- in the proportions measured from Yahoo's rostership, plus whether he gets the best player in the deal and how active he is. The yes-chance ranks offers; it is a rough estimate, not a measured rate. Each trade is priced on its own, as an alternative to the others. The numbers are from a second, larger simulation than the one that picked the trades, so the pick does not flatter them; ± is the range that simulation's own noise leaves (95%), and a trade inside it is marked toss-up.

By expected gain: the chance he says yes times the title odds you gain.

Most valuable players

Value is points above a waiver pickup at his position, summed over weeks 9-17: what he is simulated to score each week he plays, less what the pickup would. Weeks he misses (byes, injuries, a reported timeline) count nothing, so a hurt star drops down. Upside is that value in his best tenth of simulated seasons: a breakout, a bigger role, a clean bill of health. Pickup level a game: QB 14.5, RB 8.1, WR 9.3, TE 8.5, K 9.1, D/ST 13.2. RoS/g is his season value a game and Δwk its move since last week (green up, red down, yellow flat; deeper is bigger -- tap Δwk for the risers, again for the fallers), Wk this week's projection, G games expected, Range his points a week (10th-90th percentile) and Mkt what the rest of the league sees him worth a game (those three on wider screens). Tap a column to sort; your players are highlighted. Tap a player's name for his game log: points, snap share and stat line, week by week.

Each player's future is simulated (role drift, injuries, byes, the next man up taking over -- graded on 2022-2025 seasons it was not fitted to: points per game land in its middle half half the time, early form carries on as far as it really did, and what a manager can see of a player moves as much, and means as little, as a real projection did); every team starts its best lineup each week on what it could see then; the season is played on the real schedule and the playoffs on the real bracket. Rosters are held as they stand. The small ranges are 95% intervals for the simulation's own noise (Wilson): what a rerun could move the number by -- not whether the model's view of the season is right. Power is record-blind: the share of the other teams' scores a team beats in an average remaining week (all-play), from the same simulation and the same fading of team strength, so a team with a bad record and a strong roster ranks high here while its title odds stay low. Pts/wk ahead is the expected points a week for the rest of the regular season (a little closer together than raw projections: managers' waiver moves level rosters), so far what the team has scored a week in the weeks counted; a big gap between the two means the roster has changed or the points came on luck. Tap a column heading to sort.

Where this week's projections come from

Each player's number blends, where he has one from each:

  • our model and Yahoo's projection, 54% and 46%, measured on 812 graded games;
  • the betting market's implied points, 25% where books price him -- none in this week's numbers yet: books post a game's props a day or two before kickoff, the Sunday-morning run buys them, and a refresh spends no credits, so it uses only props already bought;
  • the FantasyPros consensus projection, 30% (12 of your 12 players), measured on 1395 graded games.

Each weight is the one that would have been most accurate on this season's finished games, pulled toward its starting value until enough are graded. Waiver moves, by title odds

Each pickup is priced in P(win the title) on the same simulated seasons: claiming now, against waiting and claiming only if he breaks out (you win that claim when your priority beats the other managers who also want him), less what your waiver priority is worth on future claims. Passing is not free: if he breaks out, a rival claims him, and what that does to your title odds is counted. Each move is priced on its own; make one, then refresh. Assumes about a third of active managers chase any one breakout. Injured free agents are priced as IR stashes: no roster spot until he is back, with the chance he never is.

Waiver plans: several moves together

Moves interact -- two backs chasing one lineup spot are worth less together, two dead roster spots turned into a starter and his handcuff can be worth more -- so every combination of two or three pickups and drops is screened, and the best priced in title odds against standing pat and against the best single move. Make the plan when it beats that single move by more than the simulation noise; a close call when by less.

Every 1-for-1, 2-for-1 and 1-for-2 with every team, and 2-for-2 among each side's eight most valuable players; when a deal frees one of your roster spots, the free agent who adds most fills it and is priced in. For him: he cannot see this tool, so his side is judged the way the market values players -- the platform's projection, a player's name and last season, this season so far, injuries -- in the proportions measured from Yahoo's rostership, plus whether he gets the best player in the deal and how active he is. The yes-chance ranks offers; it is a rough estimate, not a measured rate. Each trade is priced on its own, as an alternative to the others. The numbers are from a second, larger simulation than the one that picked the trades, so the pick does not flatter them; ± is the range that simulation's own noise leaves (95%), and a trade inside it is marked toss-up.

By expected gain: the chance he says yes times the title odds you gain.

Most valuable players

Value is points above a waiver pickup at his position, summed over weeks 9-17: what he is simulated to score each week he plays, less what the pickup would. Weeks he misses (byes, injuries, a reported timeline) count nothing, so a hurt star drops down. Upside is that value in his best tenth of simulated seasons: a breakout, a bigger role, a clean bill of health. Pickup level a game: QB 15.8, RB 7.2, WR 7.2, TE 7.6, K 9.5, D/ST 8.9. RoS/g is his season value a game and Δwk its move since last week (green up, red down, yellow flat; deeper is bigger -- tap Δwk for the risers, again for the fallers), Wk this week's projection, G games expected, Range his points a week (10th-90th percentile) and Mkt what the rest of the league sees him worth a game (those three on wider screens). Each player's future is simulated (role drift, injuries, byes, the next man up taking over -- graded on 2022-2025 seasons it was not fitted to: points per game land in its middle half half the time, early form carries on as far as it really did, and what a manager can see of a player moves as much, and means as little, as a real projection did); every team starts its best lineup each week on what it could see then; the season is played on the real schedule and the playoffs on the real bracket. Rosters are held as they stand. The small ranges are 95% intervals for the simulation's own noise (Wilson): what a rerun could move the number by -- not whether the model's view of the season is right. Power is record-blind: the share of the other teams' scores a team beats in an average remaining week (all-play), from the same simulation and the same fading of team strength, so a team with a bad record and a strong roster ranks high here while its title odds stay low. Pts/wk ahead is the expected points a week for the rest of the regular season (a little closer together than raw projections: managers' waiver moves level rosters), so far what the team has scored a week in the weeks counted; a big gap between the two means the roster has changed or the points came on luck. Tap a column heading to sort.
